q: The most frequently occurring fault in power systems is:
explanation: Single line-to-ground faults make up about 70–80% of faults on overhead lines (insulator flashover, trees, birds). Three-phase faults are the rarest (~5%) but usually most severe.
why: Rarest, though most severe in general.

q: The most severe fault, generally used to rate circuit breakers, is the:
explanation: A bolted 3-phase fault gives the highest fault current in most systems (an LG fault can exceed it only near solidly earthed generators with low Z_{0}).
why: Less than three-phase (≈ 0.866 × 3φ current with Z_{1} = Z_{2}).
Series faults draw less than load current.

q: Which fault is a symmetrical fault?
explanation: Only the balanced three-phase (L–L–L or L–L–L–G) fault keeps the system symmetrical, so it can be solved on a per-phase basis with positive-sequence network alone.

q: Zero-sequence currents cannot flow in:
options: A delta-connected line circuit (outside the delta)
The neutral of a grounded system
explanation: Zero-sequence currents are in phase in all three lines and need a return path (neutral/earth). They can circulate inside a delta but cannot appear in lines connected to it.
why: Earth is the return path for 3I_{0}.

q: Which sequence components are present in a line-to-line fault (no ground)?
explanation: No ground path means no zero sequence. I_{a1} = −I_{a2} = E/(Z_{1} + Z_{2}).
why: Zero sequence needs a ground connection.
Only a balanced 3-phase fault has positive sequence alone.

q: For a single line-to-ground fault, the sequence networks are connected in:
options: Positive and negative in parallel only
why: Parallel connection is for the L–L–G fault (all three) or L–L (positive and negative).

q: An unloaded generator has E = 1 p.u., Z_{1} = Z_{2} = j0.2 p.u., Z_{0} = j0.1 p.u., solidly grounded. Magnitude of the L–G fault current is:
why: 44% lower than the correct result — does not follow from the correct working.
That is the 3-phase fault current E/Z_{1}.

q: For the same generator (E = 1 p.u., Z_{1} = j0.2 p.u.), the three-phase fault current is:
why: That is the L–G value here.

q: The operator "a" in symmetrical components has the value:
why: That relates line and phase voltages.

q: Fault level at a bus is to be found. Base 100 MVA, Thevenin impedance to the fault = 0.1 p.u. Fault MVA is:
An overcurrent relay set at 125% is connected through a 400/5 A CT. For a fault current of 4000 A the plug setting multiplier (PSM) is:
why: 25% lower than the correct result — does not follow from the correct working.

q: An IDMT relay has a characteristic in which operating time:
options: Is inversely related to current at low multiples and tends to a definite minimum at high currents
explanation: Inverse Definite Minimum Time: time ∝ 1/I near pick-up, flattening to a definite minimum because the magnetic circuit saturates.

q: A directional overcurrent relay is required for:
options: Radial feeders fed from one end
explanation: When fault current can flow in either direction, relays must respond only to current flowing into the protected section.
why: Non-directional relays suffice for radial feeders.

q: Distance relays are mainly used to protect:
explanation: They measure V/I (impedance to fault) at the relay point and are standard for HV/EHV lines with zones (Zone 1 ≈ 80–90% of the line, Zone 2, Zone 3 back-up).

q: Which distance relay is best suited for long EHV transmission lines?
explanation: Mho relays are inherently directional and occupy the least R–X area, so they are least affected by power swings — preferred for long lines. Reactance relays suit short lines (unaffected by arc resistance).
why: Suitable for medium lines; not inherently directional.

q: A reactance relay is preferred for short lines because it is:
explanation: It measures only X; arc resistance (significant relative to the small impedance of short lines) does not cause under-reach.
why: Reactance relays are not inherently directional; a mho starter is used.

q: Differential protection is mainly used for:
explanation: It compares currents entering and leaving a zone (Merz–Price principle); internal faults cause a difference that operates the relay.
why: Lines use distance protection (pilot differential only for short lines).

q: Percentage (biased) differential relays are used to:
options: Prevent mal-operation due to CT mismatch during heavy through-faults
explanation: Restraint coils carrying through-current raise the operating threshold proportionally, avoiding trips from CT errors and tap changing.
why: External faults should not cause operation.

q: Transformer differential relays use second-harmonic restraint to avoid tripping on:
explanation: Inrush current is rich in second harmonic and appears on one side only; harmonic restraint blocks the relay during inrush.
why: Overfluxing is detected with 5th harmonic / V/f relays.

q: The secondary of a current transformer should never be open-circuited while the primary is carrying current because:
options: A very high voltage is induced and the core may saturate and overheat
explanation: Without secondary ampere-turns opposing the primary, all primary current magnetises the core: flux rises to saturation, inducing dangerous peak voltages and heating.
why: Primary current is set by the line load.
Secondary current becomes zero when open.

q: Standard secondary current rating of protection CTs is:
explanation: CT secondaries are 1 A or 5 A; PT (VT) secondaries are usually 110 V line-to-line.

q: A 600/5 A CT carries 450 A in its primary. Secondary current is:
SF6 is used in circuit breakers because it:
options: Is electronegative with excellent dielectric strength and arc-quenching ability
explanation: SF6 captures free electrons forming heavy ions, giving fast recovery of dielectric strength; its dielectric strength is about 2–3 times that of air at the same pressure.
why: It is costly and a potent greenhouse gas.

q: Vacuum circuit breakers are most widely used for:
explanation: Vacuum interrupters dominate distribution voltages; very fast dielectric recovery and long contact life make them ideal up to ~33–36 kV. SF6 dominates EHV.

q: In a vacuum circuit breaker the arc is sustained by:
explanation: There is no gas; the arc burns in metal vapour released from the contacts, which condenses rapidly at current zero.
why: There is no air in the interrupter.

q: Air-blast circuit breakers are mainly used for:
options: EHV systems requiring fast, repeated operation
explanation: High-pressure air blasts the arc for very fast interruption; historically used on EHV lines (now largely replaced by SF6).

q: In AC circuit breakers, the arc is interrupted mainly at:
explanation: At natural current zero the arc extinguishes; the breaker must then build dielectric strength faster than the rate of rise of restriking voltage (RRRV).
why: Interrupting at peak causes huge overvoltages (current chopping).

q: A 3-phase breaker is rated 2000 A breaking current at 132 kV. Its symmetrical breaking capacity is about:
explanation: ≈ 457 MVA

q: If the symmetrical breaking current of a breaker is 20 kA, its making current (peak) is about:
explanation: = 51 kA peak

q: An isolator (disconnector) is designed to be operated:
options: Off load, after the circuit breaker has opened
explanation: Isolators have no arc-quenching ability; they provide visible isolation for maintenance after the breaker interrupts current.
why: Normally manual or motorised on command, interlocked with the breaker.

q: Fusing factor of a fuse is defined as:
explanation: Fusing factor = minimum fusing current ÷ current rating, always > 1 (HRC fuses ≈ 1.1–1.5).

q: A lightning (surge) arrester is connected:
options: In the neutral of the generator only
explanation: It presents high impedance at normal voltage and low impedance during a surge, diverting surge current to earth and limiting voltage on equipment.
why: A series device would carry load current.

q: Modern surge arresters at substations are mostly of the:
explanation: ZnO blocks have highly non-linear V–I characteristics, so no series gap is needed and protection is fast and consistent.

q: The overhead earth (shield/ground) wire on transmission towers protects against:
options: Direct lightning strokes on phase conductors
explanation: Placed above the phase conductors, it intercepts direct strokes and drains them through the tower footing; protective (shielding) angle is typically about 30°.
why: Switching surges originate inside the system.

q: A Petersen coil (arc suppression coil) is connected between:
options: Line and earth at each tower
explanation: Its inductance is tuned to the system’s phase-to-earth capacitance (X_{L} = 1/(3ωC)), so the fault current at a single line-to-ground fault is neutralised and arcing grounds are suppressed.

q: For resonant (Petersen coil) grounding of a system whose per-phase capacitance to earth is C, the coil inductance should be:
solution: Coil current must equal capacitive fault current 3ωCV_{ph}
why: Ignores that all three phase capacitances feed the fault.

q: Arcing grounds are a problem in:
explanation: In an isolated neutral system an earth fault arc can extinguish and restrike repeatedly, building up dangerous overvoltages.

q: Earth resistance of a large power station/substation earthing system should be about:
explanation: Large stations target very low values (≈0.5 Ω for power stations, ≈1 Ω for large substations) so fault current is safely dissipated and step/touch voltages stay low.
why: Too high for stations; may be acceptable for small installations.

q: A residual current device (RCCB/ELCB) for protection of persons against shock typically trips at:
explanation: A 30 mA RCD limits shock duration so that current through the body stays below dangerous levels.
why: Far too high for personal safety.
Used for fire protection, not personal protection.

q: A Buchholz relay operates on:
explanation: It is a mechanical gas-actuated relay: gas accumulation tilts the upper float (alarm); an oil surge moves the lower float/flap (trip).

q: Reverse power relays are used to protect a generator against:
explanation: If the prime mover fails, the alternator draws power from the grid and runs as a motor, which can damage the turbine; the relay detects reverse real power.
why: Stator earth fault relays do that.

q: Negative-sequence protection of a generator guards against:
options: Unbalanced loading that overheats the rotor
explanation: Negative-sequence current produces a field rotating at twice synchronous speed relative to the rotor, inducing double-frequency currents and heating; limit is I_{2}^{2}t.

q: Auto-reclosing is used on overhead lines because:
options: Most faults are transient (≈ 80%) and clear after the line is de-energised
explanation: Flashovers from lightning, birds or branches often clear once the arc is extinguished; reclosing restores supply quickly.
why: It does not change fault current.
Cable faults are usually permanent; reclosing is avoided.

q: Recovery voltage in a circuit breaker is:
options: The voltage across contacts just before opening
The normal-frequency rms voltage appearing across the contacts after final arc extinction
explanation: Restriking voltage is the transient immediately after current zero; recovery voltage is the power-frequency voltage that remains.
why: Contacts are closed before opening (zero voltage).

q: Bus-bar protection is commonly provided by:
explanation: The sum of currents into a healthy bus is zero; high-impedance differential schemes are stable for through faults even with CT saturation.
why: Fuses are not used at HV buses.
Distance relays only give slow back-up.

q: For E = 1 p.u. and Z_{1} = Z_{2} = j0.2 p.u., the magnitude of a line-to-line fault current is about:
explanation: ≈ 4.33 p.u. (= 0.866 × three-phase value)
why: That is only the positive-sequence current.

q: A fault level of 1000 MVA at a 132 kV bus corresponds to a fault current of about:
why: 3 times too large — a typical formula slip.

q: An IDMT relay operates in 3 s at a given PSM with TMS = 1. With TMS set to 0.4 it will operate in:
why: That is the TMS, not a time.
Divides by TMS instead of multiplying.

q: A 5 A CT secondary circuit has a total burden resistance of 0.4 Ω. The burden in VA is:
explanation: = 10 VA
